name: Fibromyalgia
definition: A long-term condition that causes pain all over the body.
overview: Fibromyalgia, also called fibromyalgia syndrome, is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body. The NHS says increased sensitivity to pain, muscle stiffness, poor sleep, fatigue and difficulty concentrating are common. It is more common in women than in men and typically develops between the ages of 25 and 55, according to the NHS. The exact cause is unknown and there is no specific test, but treatments can help relieve some of the symptoms.
causes: Abnormal levels of certain chemicals in the brain are thought to be involved
Altered signalling in the nerve pathways that send and receive pain
Genetic factors, as the condition tends to run in families
Triggers such as injury, infection or stress may play a part
riskFactors: Typically developing between the ages of 25 and 55
Other conditions, especially rheumatic diseases, mood disorders or conditions that cause pain
signs: No specific laboratory or imaging abnormality identifies the condition
Widespread pain with other symptoms such as fatigue and poor sleep
complications: Depression and anxiety can accompany the condition
Other conditions may be present at the same time
diagnosis: There is no specific test for fibromyalgia, the NHS says. NIAMS says it is diagnosed mainly from widespread pain together with other symptoms. A clinician takes a history, examines the person and considers other conditions with similar symptoms.
treatment: There is no cure, and the NHS says the main treatments are exercise, talking therapies and medicines. Antidepressants are sometimes used to relieve pain. NIAMS describes a plan combining psychological and behavioural therapy, medicines and self-management such as physical exercise, yoga or tai chi. Anti-inflammatory pain relievers usually do not help the fibromyalgia itself, according to NIAMS.
prevention: The sources reviewed do not describe a way to prevent fibromyalgia; self-management steps such as staying active, good sleep habits and managing stress are described for living with it.
seekCare: The NHS advises seeing a GP, through a routine appointment, if a person thinks they have fibromyalgia. NHS-based guidance suggests getting in touch again if pain is getting worse, self-help has not helped after several weeks, or new symptoms appear. Call 999 for an emergency, and use NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment for urgent problems.

sections.heading: What is fibromyalgia?
sections.body:
Fibromyalgia, also called fibromyalgia syndrome, is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body. Versus Arthritis describes it as not a problem of the joints, bones or muscles themselves. It says that, unlike in conditions such as arthritis, the pain is not caused by visible inflammation or damage to the body. The charity adds that the exact cause is unclear.

The NHS says it is more common in women than in men and typically develops between the ages of 25 and 55. The US National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS) says that anyone can get fibromyalgia and that it affects people of all racial and ethnic backgrounds. Symptoms can change over time and vary from person to person, and they can sometimes suddenly improve or get worse. There is currently no cure, but there are treatments that help relieve some of the symptoms and make the condition easier to live with.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of fibromyalgia?
sections.body:
The NHS lists increased sensitivity to pain, muscle stiffness, poor sleep and fatigue among the common symptoms. It also describes problems with concentration and memory, known as fibro-fog, meaning difficulty concentrating or remembering things. Other health bodies describe a similar picture of widespread pain, fatigue, sleep problems and trouble with memory and concentration.

Some people also report numbness or tingling, sensitivity to light and noise, headaches and digestive problems. Depression and anxiety are also listed among the symptoms people may have. Symptoms often flare and then ease over time, which means that how a person feels can differ from one week to the next. Because the symptoms can be similar to those of a number of other conditions, the NHS says there is no specific test to confirm the diagnosis.

sections.heading: What causes fibromyalgia, and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body:
The NHS says the exact cause is unknown. It says the condition is thought to be related to abnormal levels of certain chemicals in the brain. NIAMS says brain imaging studies and other research have found evidence of altered signalling in the nerve pathways that send and receive pain. The NHS adds that genes and triggers such as injury, infection or stress may play a part.

NIAMS says the condition tends to run in families, so genetic factors are likely to contribute, although the specific genes are not well identified. It also says researchers think environmental factors play a role. Having other conditions, especially rheumatic diseases, mood disorders or conditions that cause pain, may make fibromyalgia more likely, according to NIAMS. Versus Arthritis notes a common link with arthritis, a traumatic event, and mental health and wellbeing.

sections.heading: How is fibromyalgia diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no specific test for fibromyalgia. NIAMS says the diagnosis is made mainly from widespread pain together with other symptoms, and that there are currently no specific laboratory or imaging tests for it. In practice a clinician takes a history, carries out an examination and considers other conditions that could explain the symptoms.

The CDC notes that a person may need to see different health care providers to rule out other conditions with similar symptoms. NIAMS says doctors may also ask about other conditions, because some people with fibromyalgia have other diseases at the same time. NIAMS says primary care providers manage most patients, with pain specialists also involved in some cases. NICE lists fibromyalgia as an example of chronic primary pain, meaning long-term pain that is not better explained by another condition.

sections.heading: How is fibromyalgia treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says the main treatments are exercise, talking therapies and medicines. It says antidepressants are sometimes used to relieve pain. NIAMS describes a plan that typically combines psychological and behavioural therapy, medicines and self-management approaches such as physical exercise and movement therapies like yoga or tai chi. The CDC says talk therapy such as cognitive behavioural therapy can help people learn strategies to deal with pain, stress and negative thoughts.

NIAMS says some drugs can ease pain and improve sleep, and that drugs used for depression may also work in fibromyalgia even when a person is not depressed. It adds that anti-inflammatory pain relievers usually do not help the fibromyalgia itself, because the condition does not involve tissue inflammation. Versus Arthritis says a doctor may only recommend drug treatment once options such as exercise, psychological therapy or acupuncture have been tried. For chronic primary pain, NICE guideline NG193 recommends offering a supervised group exercise programme to people aged 16 and over, and considering an antidepressant for adults after a full discussion of the benefits and risks.

sections.heading: What can help with living with fibromyalgia day to day?
sections.body:
Versus Arthritis describes pacing as balancing activity and rest, so that a person does not overdo things on good days or feel worse after doing too much. The CDC lists learning self-management skills, staying physically active, keeping a healthy weight, protecting the joints, having good sleep habits and managing stress as steps people can take. Versus Arthritis says poor sleep appears to be a significant factor in fibromyalgia and that getting enough good-quality sleep is an important part of treatment.

Heat packs and relaxation techniques are commonly suggested for easing symptoms. For fibro-fog, practical tips include writing things down and breaking tasks into smaller steps. The NHS points to Fibromyalgia Action UK, a charity with a helpline, as a source of support.

sections.heading: When should someone see a doctor about fibromyalgia?
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP if a person thinks they have fibromyalgia, and a routine GP appointment is the usual route.

NHS-based guidance suggests getting back in touch if pain is getting worse, if self-help measures have not helped after several weeks, if prescribed medicine is not helping, or if new symptoms appear. It also says that anyone who thinks they may be depressed should get help from a GP. If someone feels in immediate danger from thoughts of harming themselves, calling 999 is the route, and NHS 111 (mental health option) or Samaritans on 116 123, free at any time, can also be used. For sudden severe symptoms that do not fit the usual pattern, such as chest pain or weakness on one side, call 999; NHS 111 or a same-day GP appointment is the route for urgent problems that are not emergencies.

faqs.a: There is currently no cure for fibromyalgia, the NHS says. Treatments can help relieve some of the symptoms and make the condition easier to live with. The main treatments the NHS describes are exercise, talking therapies and medicines, and symptoms can sometimes improve or get worse suddenly.

faqs.q: Is fibromyalgia the same as arthritis?
faqs.a: No. Versus Arthritis says fibromyalgia is not a problem of the joints, bones or muscles themselves. It says the pain is not caused by visible inflammation or damage to the body, unlike in conditions such as arthritis. NIAMS says the two can occur together, since having other conditions, especially rheumatic diseases, may make fibromyalgia more likely.

faqs.q: Does fibromyalgia show up on blood tests or scans?
faqs.a: NIAMS says there are currently no specific laboratory or imaging tests for fibromyalgia, and the NHS says there is no specific test. Diagnosis rests mainly on widespread pain and other symptoms. Doctors may also consider other conditions with similar symptoms.

The NHS lists exercise among the main treatments for fibromyalgia. NIAMS includes physical exercise and movement therapies such as yoga or tai chi in the self-management part of a treatment plan. Versus Arthritis describes pacing, balancing activity and rest, as a way to avoid doing too much on good days.
